reviews.text: the game is fun, until the first what I guess could be called "big boss" no matter how you build your character, which by the way is pretty random, you cant deal enough damage to boss, who has a stacking, before the stack effect that you get from his long range spawn kills you, not to mention that the second time he uses his " ultimate move" nearly every tile to and away from him becomes effected. once you reach 10 stacks you immediately die and there is no possible way to avoid getting 10 stacks. they need to nerf this boss because as the game is now, it blocks all progress. wait till full release or a patch that addresses this issue.

Its a good game but needs balancing, if you like getting stuck in fail loops, this game is for you!! The skill crafting is great, when you are given the tools to do so, but the game overwhelms you with spawns, and your damage output is not enough to keep up. The AP point mechanic is a nice challenging change, but yet again, you spend 1 point, and if you have 5 enemies, you have 5 AP coming back at you, now add spawners that are scattered all over the map, that spawn constantly, and you have to use AP points just to get to them, by the time you get across the map, they've spawned 3 more enemies, now at this point you spend 1 AP and have 10+ AP coming back at you. You will reach a unique "mind" where you just get stuck there in a fail loop, you get nothing to help you after each fail, except knowledge of foes...pointless if you don't have the tools needed. Another draw back is that you cant attack diagonally, but there are foes that can <exploders-also on this point, they dont have to use AP to detonate themselves, so they get to use all AP for movement and still explode(with massive AoE btw> spend that extra AP point to get lined up, the enemy get to line up with you for free!

--- Edit after 55h of EA and 20h of 1.0 I just finished the storyline and... wow wow wow... wow... It s atrocious. It's really really bad. I change my review and DONT RECOMMEND. For a game about getting better, the main message presented is exactly what NOT to do if you ever want to deal with your s***. It s moralizing, condescending, pain-centered, cut from emotions, analysis on top of analysis... exhausting. And just for that, I don't recommend this game (more details at the end). Now, that being said, the visuals are nice and the mechanics could have been fun. But, the story sucks and the progression doesn't favor exploring mechanics early. It took 20h to finish the story, and I took my time. I thought that some skills were not balanced and allowed me to just roll on every mob and boss except the last one (got it at the 3rd time). Too easy for my taste and repetitive. The reason why the skills looked imbalanced is because I min-maxed skills that don't scale much late game in favor of consistent damage early. If you want to go beyond the story, it gets way harder and it would require some other strats to win. I don't see the point in doing more of the same, just to finally have some variety. I would have prefer to have those late-game builds viable earlier, to have more diversity during the story. It would have make me think instead of just one-shot every mobs but the bosses. In summary, the graphics are good but can't fix a bad story, and the mechanics are fun but can't fix a progression that forces you to stay longer for no other reason than exploring the mechanics. No thanks. --- In more words about the theme For a game about healiing, the main story revolves around pain, morality and duty. In this game you deal with problems by having them removed by someone else, instead of you making your way through them. The results is equal to a trepanation: the "patients" apparently barely function once they are "wantless" and become a weight for their closed ones. There is no ownership, no understanding, no flowering, no joy, no celebration... the whole process of resolving personal issues is completely missed. As the main character, you are the one making others go like zombies. What a thrill! At the end of the story, I thought they would flip it back, present the whole story has the worst possible way to go about it and shine a new light. But no, they doubled down. When it s already bleak and moralizing, the "resolution" is all about duty and cutting off bad thoughts instead of dealing with them. More repression, yeah! I was hoping a game who decided to tackle this kind of subject ("getting better/ therapy/ healing") would actually open things up, instead of presenting the usual BS. For example, "wantless" is not "need-less". It makes no sense that wantless-people can't take care of their basic needs. They would be even more capable to do so, because they have no wants to distract them from their needs. Depicting wantless people as zombies just show the devs haven't look into the matter much. It's disappointing, to me, to name a game with something you don't understand. Pretentious.

This game is ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ brutal for the first few levels, because it is designed around you having a lot of options of how to approach each fight. But you don't get those options in the first 7 or so levels. So it is setup for you to fail/not fully succeed. And then, it forces you into a tutorial whenever you start over. Because the first 3 or so maps are fully on rails, locked in to teach you. So I have to sit through 20+ minutes of locked tutorial if I have to restart, or if I want to play a different build. And the one time I had the patience to get past the early game, the difficulty spiked so hard on an optional bonus that I died and failed. It's very poorly balanced through and through.

The most surprising&satisfying diablo-like looter game of the year! 本年度最令人意外和惊喜的暗黑类刷宝游戏! i don't have to reiterate how great this game is, the rating points states the truth already. at start, i hate this game being difficult to play, then i realize, Being difficulty and challenging is just what life&reality is for mental illness tortured patients, and for psychiatrists. Game tries to awaken our attention and care to mentally-ill patients, it wins my utmost respect! Please support multi-languages in the follow-up, this game deserves to shine! One small suggestion is that we go to different facilities/towns as game advance, but the look of these new places are always the same. it should be slightly different in each location to be able to differentiate. Also, the 1st boss fight is an absolute downer, it's mandatory, it's very well-calculated boss fight when player has extremely limited resources. The worst part is there is no- "surrender, try other maps , and come back and try again" later. so the worst is, if we can't pass the boss, game is stuck 4ever!

I just want to play. Shove it all into the first couple hours or spread it out over 20- I don't care. Stop interrupting me.

In Wantless you play as Eiris, a sci-fi dystopian mindshrink of sorts, with the task of "healing" your patients' mind, via an turn based tactical action point combat system, that sees you battling weird daemons of the mind from various patients. On top of that is tacked on a fiddly and trite RPG system, boasting 170 perks, but it's the usual fare of +5% and +10% marginal effects, why are designers still doing this in 2024? There's also obscure loot and the usual assortment of damage types, but with little guidance for the application of each, this you must discover yourself through trial and error, and reading tooltips and slowly uncovering the attacks and weaknesses of each boss and enemy types, something which must be done through repeat plays and endless failures. That's well and all, but the game thinks its a rogue lite, so there's no options for manual saves, which just leads to far too much tedium in an uphill presentation, and perhaps if you were to persevere and overcome your own daemons of the mind caused by the game, there is perhaps a unpolished gem underneath. But I fear you'll end up as the patients you try to cure before that happens. Wantless is a novel attempt and a cool concept, that could have climbed higher, if not for some questionable design decisions.

I played the demo and I liked the concept of the game. Purchased full game after release. Yet with every session I was becoming more and more disappointed. I think the ambition of the authors wasn't matched by the quality of execution, and I'm not talking about bugs (although some are there). The frustration is coming from overly engineered management which tries to grasp some modern features from MMO games (I'm talking about forge/fusion) as well as the reward system, which is by all means inferior, given the difficulty of the combat. The combat is a huge failure, and it's not because of imbalance. Some games do have complex mechanics, and the best examples are very careful about keeping its players knowledgeable and informed at all times. Wantless has a GLOSSARY. And it's the most useless glossary I've ever seen in a game. It doesn't tell you about nearly half of things like tiers, disciplines, types of effects, etc. You won't find any help on how different types of damage work with counter-effects, resistances, etc. Basically you're thrown into a huge pool of skills, effects, tiers, modifiers, resistances, buffs, debuffs, upgrades, quality and other mumbo-jumbo. And you have to figure it out yourself. Now, back to the problem with combat, the game is designed to have multiple skillsets so you're kinda expected to come to battle prepared, with the most efficient skills against given enemies. Does this concept work? ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. You gotta learn by heart all that little nonsense. And I have no ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ remaining capacity of my brain to deduct, analyse and memorise all of that. Every time it's just a guess about which enemies would appear in the next transposition and WHAT ON EARTH I HAVE TO EQUIP MYSELF WITH TO BE ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ EFFICIENT. Pardon, but this is not rage but frustration. And you know what? I'm not even stuck here. I'm slowly progressing and 12 hrs into the game I continue to unlock the map and move through the story. Why'd you say am I frustrated? It's because 12 hrs into the game I feel like I'm still playing the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ tutorial and the hints are waaay overdue. I feel no certainty, no support, no foundation for anything. Every new game day is pretty much random and I gotta rely on one and the same skillset that somehow works. And the way it works is pathetic. No matter what I get after battle, the situation remains the same. It's like playing chess with random people in the street. I mentioned poor reward system. Amongst the issues with UI, lack of information and overall complexity, that is the worst. The golden rule of any game - video or not - says that the effort must be matched with the reward. I've been waiting for a long time where I will get some feeling of accomplishment here or at least a big juicy unique buff. It never happened so far. Fun fact: those unique equipment items seem to always have some debuff which will diminish the value. So, it's kinda yeah nah after each battle, over and over again. Well, I'm OKfor the devs to take my money and spend it making a better game next time, listening to my (and others') complaints. With Wantless, however, I'm done for now. Consider me completely transposed so I no longer want any of this doubtful entertainment.

An unbalanced, dull and unintuitive game. Don't let the skill tree fool you - there is virtually no development choice here, and skill crafting boils down to creating one or two combat skills, one healing skill, one jerk and a couple skills of your choice. There is a plot, a couple lines every two hours. The whole RPG element boils down to +15% poison damage or -4% to the cost of a skil. Enemies are always plentiful and their abilities are simple and extremely nasty - a couple arena shooters will cheerfully run away from you while attacking you for 15-20% of your health, and mushrooms will slow you down and summon friends. I really tried to understand this game, but judging by the fact that the game after the release received 2 mini patches, the developers just threw their project in the release and left to do something else.

I don't wanna discourage others. Game just throws serious inescapable and unpredictable scenario on your way. That alone is so discouraging for me after long grind. I see no incentive to start the game again and play, knowing the unpredictable random destruction bosses inflict. My recommendation is for those with significant pain tolerance. Cheers

It's like XCom if everything about XCom were needlessly over complicated to the point where EVERY room involves reading multiple pages of enemy and skill descriptions to avoid being one shot by random ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. I don't know who this game is for or why they find it enjoyable. Do developers really think that "more systems" means "better game"?? It's okay to have enemies, especially in the very early stages of your game, NOT have seven unique skills. There can be vanilla mobs. If EVERY enemy has a pile of unique stuff going on *no* enemy feels unique; it's just another exercise in tedium to discern which ways this particular one will ♥♥♥♥ you over.

I wanted to like this game because I like tactical combat games. But sadly, I can't recommend this. Bosses (and to a lesser extent, rare enemies) are huge HP sponges. It's never been fun when a game add HP to enemies as a way to raise difficulty. It is possible to soft lock your game (or even potentially hard lock yourself). When the game forces you to fight a boss encounter, and will let you do nothing else. This means that if you are too weak, or have a bad build and can't reset, you're just stuck. Also, the game is very repetitive. It's just the same handful of small, flat maps with a couple of random tiles. What little story the game has, is very uninteresting. All of the game is about "going into the head" of a pool of random 3-4 people that are available each day. Every once in a while, you may get unique person with some bit of backstory. But it doesn't really matters. Nothing will hook you. It's just a transparent gimmick to make you chose what random rewards you want. There is no grand story and interesting sights. This is basically a random fight generator. It feel like they build the combat engine, and gave up on creating the rest of the game. So if you like a game all about getting into random fights on a flat grid, then go for it. Otherwise, this game is a skip, in my opinion. There are plenty of tactical games that are way better than this.

It's incredibly grindy. You fight what feels like the same combats over and over, making only tiny progress after each mission. Sometimes it's hard to tell if you've made any progress at all. It's too bad, since the underlying system allows for enormous customization. You build spells by combining a range/area of effect, spell effects, and spell cost. You can mash together all sorts of things, and create all sorts of specialization. I get the impression the game would be a lot better if there were a large, knowledgeable community out there talking strategies. Instead, every time I run into a wall where I simply cannot handle a specific unique patient, there's no one to offer advice. So I end up abandoning most of them, and never returning. The story is frankly disturbing. The "battles" you're fighting are inside people's heads, removing things from their minds. Sometimes this is good, like removing addictions, but fairly often it seems you're inflicting brain damage. It doesn't matter than the patients request it, often what you're doing is objectively an atrocity. Take the "wantless" of the game's title. These are people who have voluntarily gotten lobotomized so they don't care about anything. You do this now and then, remove people's wants and desires. I think I put far too much time into this game, hoping it was going to click eventually.

Couple of hours in. Like it a lot. Not like a random game from a gamer perspective, but more like appreciation of how it's done game-dev-wise. World and activities are minimalistic but pleasant. Help is done as on-call window with search and filtering. Combat is very easy to understand. Craftable skills seem fun. And overall it's fun and interesting to play. I would highly recommend to take a look if you are making your own game/pet project, I think there are some stuff to learn here.

This is a really good strategy game! I'm very impressed with the originality of the concept. The idea of a doctor for the mind using technology and skill to relieve all the negative emotions and feelings of their patients is totally awesome. Transposition! It reminds me a little of a Shadowrun cybercombat hacking process. Your avatar enters the patients mind, armed to the teeth with a variety of skills and methods to choose from. You design all of your skills in every way. Range, Effect, and Cost are all up to you. It reminded me of Morrowind's spell crafting freedom and variety, which is honestly the best ever, so that's one hell of a compliment from me. You must balance power with cost and build a skill set to work through the challenges of each quest. Each patient has a goal for you like defeat a boss, collect memories, or defeat a certain number of "monsters" all while trying to stay alive and collecting synapses to improve your abilities. The story-line was succinct and decent, I liked it. I didn't feel like I had to skip through lots of dialog which was really appreciated and very rare these days. The heroine struggling with morality and her decisions of who to help was a high level of thinking, I enjoyed. The complexity of the skill crafting and mind tree were more than enough to keep my brain locked in. Even after beating the game's main quest there is another layer of depth and growth available. Not to mention additional quests and challenges to conquer. I highly recommend this game. I feel like this is a sleeper because I've never heard anyone talk about it. Thank you Devs, you hit a home run with this one.

Fun game if you like tactical RPGs with deep skill customization (lots of abilities to craft and a massive perk tree). Each room feels like a strategic puzzle, though it can get a bit repetitive at times. The build variety is incredible. If you enjoy smart, challenging turn-based combat, this one’s a must-play.
An interesting game that deserves more recognition than it received.

I can already tell this game is going to be grindy, but no it has to go that next step. If real life happens and you are in the middle of a run? Too bad you have to start over because despite the design being level based, it doesn't save between levels.

It's neat, though a bit rough around the edges. The star of the show here is the build variety. You have a big skill tree, with interconnected nodes, and the ability to build your own active abilities by combining elements that make up the shape/range, the effect, and the cost, so there's really a lot of possibilities here. Unfortunately the game is fairly repetitive and grindy, so getting deeper into your build can be a bit frustrating at times. There's also the way AP (action points) work, which I wasn't fond of - basically, the amount of AP you use in a turn is the amount of AP enemies will get when their turn comes around. It's an interesting idea, and thematically appropriate, but in practice it varies wildly between extremely abusable and really punishing, which gets frustrating. As for the story, it's rather barebone and ends abruptly. It's still a good game overall, but I don't see myself sinking much more time than I already did in it.

Absolutely brilliant game. Honestly one of the best I played in a long time. Definitely recommend it to anybody who is into tactical RPGs. I love it! In this unique tactical RPG, you can craft your skills by combining shape of skill, up to five effects and relating costs. Each of the different components can have up to 4 additional bonus 'nodes' which allow you further customisation / powering up of your skills. By investing some time, you can create extremely overpowered skills. On the flip side, this does make the start seem a bit overwhelming, which, to me, explains the reviews where people complain they can't see their progression. I disagree with this since it means they didn't choose the right strategy on their skills, however, understanding how to develop the skills will take time. Only real bad thing I can say about this game is that I wish there was more to do. After 60 hours, I beat all bosses in the game and got all achievements. I would love to put more hours in the game but there's nothing left to achieve.

I like tactical games and this one scratched an itch for me real hard. it has one of the more unique systems to allow for creating your own attacks which was a lot of fun to play around with but also lots of character growth options to make the combat strategies varied and unique. There is also a system of how the the enemies only get to do as many moves/action points as you use. this system was both unique and added lots of tactical options which just made the game an absolute joy to play. cant wait to see what else you guys come up with

Fun game. Complicated crafting system that can take a while to get a hang of, but is rewarding. Would love it if they were still updating or still development active, but worth playing. There is an endgame that can suck you in if you want to keep improving your build and challenging yourself.
A very interesting game. The gameplay was fun and engaging. However, like most games nowadays, I found it to get repetitive. Story was good and really liked the different styles of gameplay!

Brutally difficult game, but a fun challenge with lots of different ways to build your skills and equipment to match your play style. I've been mainly cheesing with 'Wall' that creates shield and then while the enemy has not detected me I just max out shields (max is equivalent to your health)... Only at Tier 2 patients so far though ... some patients are detected right from the start so then you need major burst damage ability.

Loved the tactical depth of the game. And the artwork. Story was okay. The post-game options were neat, too! Had fun for 40 hours, no time-padding or anything. No grinding needed. Once you get stuck, you re-think your strategy and create new skills. Amazing concept!

Gameplay this good as no right also having an interesting concept. ok, so let's break it down. gameplay - absolutely loved it. lots of different interacting elements and mechanics, lots of meaningful customizations. you make meaningful progress upgrading your build between runs, which makes the grind of the battles themselves fun - you have a stronger build every time, stacking more buffs and status effects, getting exponentially better. I hate grinding, absolutely hate it, i'm always looking for novelty and new experiences. so at 117 hours... i got my fair share of novelty from this. concept - changing who a person is by removing their wants. damn. would you want to... not want something? if any unfulfill want is a pain, you can remove all pain by removing all wants. what's left of you then? what could you make of yourself? what if you instead add wants, create your own ambitions? now, it's interesting in the game, but hella under-developed. maybe it seems so because the idea has endless potential, but I just feel like we're exploring only the surface. plenty to think about, not a lot to experience in the game. still, great concept.

really good if you like turn-based isometric rpgs and a high difficulty level. once i got how the mechanics work (craft-your-own-skills) it was hard to put the game down. it's a little haunting, but i like that. :D very addictive, highly recommended!
Underrated, can't wait to play more
One of the best games iv played. I love that you can fully craft your own skills together. The tutorial is a little bit long and too much at the start, but you can just skip it all.
Fun game with an interesting skill crafting system

I have no idea how I missed this game, but I am really glad I saw a friend playing it and gave this one a spin. This game has so much of what I like in a game. Tremendous build flexibility. The idea of building your own skills is remarkable and the way they lay out the systems for you is excellent. The design of the levels and bosses is well done and the volume of different kinds of things you can run into is really impressive. It took me about 20 hours to get through the main story quest and the post-game content has just opened up for me laying out tons of new skill components and bosses to chase. The volume of content here is quite impressive. This game is a difficult game that speaks to experienced tactical RPG players (if the achievements are to be believed, less than 10% of the players have made it through the final boss). If you are a player that has a lot of experience with Tac RPGs and enjoys complex systems and options, you are going to have an excellent time here. This game feels like it is a love letter to that niche audience of players and probably isn't as generally accessible as a result of that. I can see casual players getting overwhelmed by this one very easily and only recommend it to veterans of the genre.

This was an absolute unexpected gem. I almost didn't go for the game since when I see something like "customizable skills" I just assume it's going to be broken degenerate cheesed combos. I ended up with a game I liked in pretty much every way, including some unexpected ones. When's the last time I remember reading all the flavor text on every enemy because I think it's genuinely cool? Where to even start... 1. This is definitely a game I think is a textbook great game for experienced genre players. The way the system of "enemies get as much AP as you yourself spent" mixes things up is fantastic if you're already numb to repetitive tactical mechanics. The mix of enemies spending AP normally, doing turn-timed charge up actions, etc make for tons of unique puzzles. The idea of approaching non-boss fights in stealth where you can spent 5 AP a turn to move around, buff up, position summons or such before forced to start combines interesting with getting timed buffs after each fight. The core loop is just meaningfully unique and it's refreshing to figure out all the ways to abuse it. Even small mechanics like "the first turn you summon an ally their initiative goes at the end, while on future turns they go right after you" are perfectly tuned to make things interesting and make you think about your choices in ways unlike most games. 2. The crafting was something I borderline considered a negative when I read it. "Skill crafting" is something I read as 'unbalanced as heck' and I'm absolutely shocked at how smooth and intuitive it is and how well balanced. One of my first skills was a simple "enemy takes damage when moving + push the enemy". Another was applying the debuff "hurt this target when you spend AP" and "hurt this target when they take damage from other sources", and it got WILDLY more complex from there while always being something I hand-crafted every piece of and understand the roles. You can have 10 skills each one with 1 targeting shape, up to 5 effects, and 1 cooldown/cost property, and the effects/targeting modes are as varied as you'd hope. 3. The gradual ramp-up of complexity, from the gates in your skill tree and its powerful passives, to powerful unique gear/crafting parts, to many of the more nuanced and stronger enemies is great. Every 5 or 10 hours you'll feel like everything has escalated and you've mastered new levels of systems, and then it escalates even more, straight into the post-game. The pacing is just excellent. 4. I actually genuinely liked the story. It's a great example of how you don't need a lot of story to have good story - the setting of like "post-apocalyptic psychosurgeon who removes fears, desires or memories manifesting as monsters" is already really cool, and yet rather than some lofty globe-trotting conspiracy, the core of the main story is actually pretty personal with a clear arc and some bold high points and sick boss fights. ---- This isn't the sort of game I see many people putting 300 hours into, although I imagine you could. But the important thing is just that it genuinely stands out from a lot of other mid-tier indie tactical roguelike whatever stuff with a unique core loop and excellent content variety that's paced perfectly. The only real criticism I have is that a lot of the gear/ability crafting components you loot can be a bit busy, you don't have a way to sell/deconstruct from the post-run screen, and on the same note because it's so busy you'll focus on getting/keeping stuff relevant to your main strategy, which means you probably won't set aside a lot of stuff that might eventually be useful if you wanted to try out alternate specs. Out of myself and a couple of friends who played the game ,we all ended up sticking to a single general spec our entire playtime, which is a shame since we all played totally DIFFERENT specs and had very different experiences. I focused on DoT-applying summons and was great at grinding down bosses, for instance. But it felt like since i was focused on buying/keeping gear relevant to Afflictions and Summons it would've taken even more effort for me to figure out how to pivot my build to, I dunno, stealth sniper or melee tank or some of the weirder stuff like buffing-via-self-debuffs. But maybe you'll try out all that, the game's worth it.

Really fun tactical game. Leveling up, making your own spells, modifying items, etc. is all great. Plenty of interesting enemies and abilities to keep combat fresh. The psychological theme is actually well done, much better than I was expecting. The systems are easy to understand, the game just has its own thematic terminology that you'll learn. Tooltips and some observational skills are enough to figure everything out satisfyingly. It is a very forgiving game, but not overly easy.

A game crafted with great care, full of lovely details. I particularly liked the forge system, which lets you create and customise the abilities you take into battle. Unfortunately, it didn’t quite click for me, but it’s a quality game and I enjoyed it while it lasted.

I played some of the demo a ways back, and coming back to this now, while I haven't finished the main campaign it's clear this game has a lot of depth. Constructing an effective set of skills and the shear number of options and modifications, this has value to at least anyone who loves playing a satisfying tactics-type RPG to at least try. There's also the world this exists in. Initially it gives netrunner vibes, but it's actually closer to Psychonauts in terms of what the characters are doing. I appreciate the details in this game, like MtG, even the common enemies have enemy descriptions. Everything flows into the setting and there's a clear moral plot question that I am excited to see develop. Considering this game is frequently on sale for pretty accessible price tag, I can easily recommend this to roguelike and tactical RPG fans.
